cards.explanation: The answer is eat or drink. Verse 12 says the plotters bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. I think this is a heavy part of the story, friends. Their oath is tied to eating and drinking.
The answer is forty. Verse 13 says more than forty of them were involved in this plot. More than forty means the number was bigger than forty, bakers. That's a whole lot of men for one plan.

The answer is to ask the commander to bring Paul down. In verses 14 and 15 the plotters go to the chief priests and elders and tell them to have the Sanhedrin petition the commander to bring Paul down. The Sanhedrin is the Jewish council. The whole plan hangs on that one request.

The answer is True. Verse 15 says the request is to be made on the pretext of examining his case more carefully. A pretext is a cover story, friends. Right after that they say, “We are ready to kill him on the way.”

The answer is on the way down. In verse 15 the plotters say, "We are ready to kill him on the way." The way means the trip as Paul is brought down to the Sanhedrin. They plan to ambush him along the road.

The answer is that he goes into the barracks and tells Paul. Verse 16 says Paul's nephew, his sister's son, heard about the plot, went into the barracks and told Paul. He walked right in with the news. Good thing somebody did, friends.
The answer is False. Paul doesn't go to the commander himself. He calls one of the centurions in verse 17 and asks him to take the young man to the commander. The nephew carries the news in.

The answer is tomorrow. In verse 20 the nephew tells the commander the Jews will ask him to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow. So the commander hears about it ahead of time, bakers. That's a head start.

The answer is False. The nephew says, "Do not let them persuade you, because more than forty men are waiting to ambush him." (Acts 23:21) He also says they've bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they've killed Paul. He's pleading with the commander to say no.

The answer is don't tell anyone you reported this. In verse 22 the commander instructs the young man, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me.” The text doesn't give his reason, friends. It only gives the instruction.

The answer is False. Verse 23 has the commander tell two centurions to prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. That's nowhere near a handful, bakers. Claudius Lysias, the commander, is taking no chances.
The answer is Caesarea. In verse 23 the commander says to go to Caesarea. Verse 24 says to take Paul safely to Governor Felix, and in verse 33 the horsemen deliver him to the governor in Caesarea.

The answer is False. The commander says in verse 23 to go to Caesarea in the third hour of the night. That's a night departure, not a daylight one, friends. Paul leaves under the stars, not in the middle of the day.
The answer is Governor Felix. Verse 24 says to take Paul safely to Governor Felix. A governor is the Roman official in charge of the region. Felix is the man at the end of the road, friends.

The answer is that he had learned Paul was a Roman citizen. Verse 27 has Lysias write that he came with his troops to rescue Paul, for he had learned that Paul is a Roman citizen. Lysias is the commander's name, bakers. That's how he tells it to Felix.

The answer is questions about their own law. Verse 29 has Lysias write that the accusation involved questions about their own law. He also writes that he found no charge worthy of death or imprisonment. That's what he tells Felix in the letter, friends.
The answer is False. Lysias writes in verse 29, "…there was no charge worthy of death or imprisonment." That's the letter Felix reads, bakers. Neither death nor prison fits what Lysias says he found.

The answer is True. Verse 30 has Lysias write that he instructed Paul's accusers to present their case against him before Felix. He tells Felix that in the letter, friends. The accusers have been told where to go.

The answer is just the horsemen. Verse 32 says that the next day the soldiers returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with Paul. So the big crowd heads home, and the horsemen carry on with him, friends. Then verse 33 says the horsemen arrived in Caesarea and presented Paul to the governor.

The answer is Cilicia. Felix reads the whole letter and then asks one plain question: what province is Paul from? Short question, short answer, bakers: Cilicia (v34). Then he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.”

The answer is that Felix will hear his case when the accusers arrive. In verse 35 Felix says, "I will hear your case when your accusers arrive." Then he orders Paul kept under guard in Herod's Praetorium, friends. The case has to wait for the accusers to show up.
